newsitem.title: KENYA: Patchwork of groups, alliances in Zaire conflict.
newsitem.headline: Patchwork of groups, alliances in Zaire conflict.

text.p: The conflict in Zaire, Africa's second largest country, is between a mixture of alliances based mainly on ethnicity and regional interests. Here are the outlines of the main groups and how they are linked:

-- The rebel ALLIANCE OF DEMOCRATIC FORCES FOR LIBERATION OF CONGO-ZAIRE (ADFL) now controls much of eastern Zaire, including the towns of Uvira, Kamanyola, Bukavu, Goma and Beni. ADFL commanders say they have also taken Bunia, Kamituga, Mwenga and Walikale and that their forces are now knocking on the doors of Kisangani, the largest city in the area.

The alliance is made up of four political parties with a history of opposition to ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko. It includes the BANYAMULENGE, a community of about 300,000 ethnic Tutsis who moved to the area from Rwanda as long as 200 years ago but were denied Zairean citizenship in 1981.

The alliance was born out of a Zairean campaign to force the Banyamulenge back to Rwanda. Although the Banyamulenge triggered the war, they are now outnumbered in the alliance almost six to one by local tribes. The alliance leader is veteran opposition leader Laurent Kabila, a comrade-in-arms of the late Latin American revolutionary leader Che Guevara.
-- The BANYARWANDA, literally "people of Rwanda", include the Banyamulenge and anyone else in eastern Zaire whose origins were in Rwanda, whether Hutus, Tutsis or the Twa minority.

When colonial powers drew borders in the Great Lakes region in the late 19th and early 20th century some Banyarwanda found themselves within the borders of the Belgian Congo (now Zaire), others in Uganda. In the 1920s and 1930s many Rwandans were taken to work on plantations in the Belgian Congo, and many Rwandans crossed to Masisi, Zaire, as economic migrants.
Fighting between the local Banyarwanda, fleeing Rwandan Hutus and local Zaireans was concentrated in the Masisi region earlier this year, before the Banyamulenge revolt.
-- The ZAIREAN ARMY, a notoriously ill-disciplined force, reinforced its presence in eastern Zaire in September after confrontation with the Banyamulenge.

When they suffer a military defeat or lose comrades, the troops frequently rampage through civilian centres, shooting in the air, looting vehicles and stealing to augment their small and rarely paid salaries.

-- Two ZAIREAN MILITIAS, the Bangilima and the Mai-Mai, have a strong background of witchcraft. A mix of local Zairean tribes including the Hunde, they oppose the Banyarwanda and have fought both Tutsis and Hutus. They now have a tactical alliance with the Tutsis but could turn against them. The Bangilima are mainly from Lubero area. The Mai-Mai are so called because they say bullets fired at them will magically turn into water (mai).

-- An estimated 1.1 million RWANDAN HUTU REFUGEES fled their homeland in 1994 during the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs. Most were housed in crowded camps around Goma, Bukavu and Uvira in eastern Zaire, with others in equally crowded camps in western Tanzania. About 500,000 have returned home since the fighting.
-- Eastern Zaire was also refuge for an estimated 40,000 former RWANDAN HUTU GOVERNMENT TROOPS now on the run after being routed by the rebel alliance.
-- An estimated 140,000 BURUNDIAN HUTU REFUGEES lived mainly in camps north of Uvira near Burundi's western border. They scattered when rebels took control of Uvira in October.
About 30,000 returned to Burundi, others fled across Lake Tanganyika in boats to Tanzania but 100,000 are missing.

-- The 54,000-strong RWANDA PATRIOTIC ARMY is dominated by the country's Tutsi minority, which seized power in July 1994 and ended the genocide launched by the Hutu majority three months earlier. The army is backing the rebels in eastern Zaire.

-- Zaire has accused the UGANDAN ARMY of occupying the Zairean towns of Beni and Kasindi. The link, from Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni to Rwandan military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame to the Banyamulenge who fought alongside Kagame's forces in 1994, is at the heart of claims by Zaire that Rwanda and Uganda back the rebels.
